one_liner: JSON Schema-driven binary JSON format; its prototype matched or beat Protobuf, Avro, MessagePack on encoded size across 27 documents.
what_it_does: JSON BinPack converts JSON documents to a compact binary form and back. It has a schema-driven mode and a self-describing schema-less mode (ANY_PACKED_TYPE_TAG_BYTE_PREFIX) used when no schema constraint applies. A build-time compiler (sourcemeta::jsonbinpack::compile) canonicalizes a JSON Schema 2020-12 and rewrites it in place into an 'encoding schema'; load() turns that into an Encoding, Encoder::write(json, encoding) writes to a std::ostream, and Decoder::read(encoding) returns a sourcemeta::core::JSON. It is not a drop-in for any baseline: you write JSON Schemas instead of .proto, .fbs or .avsc files, and your data must be in Sourcemeta Core's JSON type.
how_it_is_fast: It does not make serialization faster; it makes output smaller by turning schema constraints into bit-level choices. Bounded integers (minimum/maximum/multipleOf) become an offset from the minimum in one byte or a Base-128 varint (ZigZag when unbounded), enums become a one-byte or varint index (zero bytes for the first choice of a top-level enum), const costs zero bytes, and decimals become a ZigZag varint of their digits plus the decimal-point position instead of an 8-byte IEEE double. Strings of 3 or more bytes already seen in the stream become a backward offset (dedup cache capped at 20 MiB), and schema-less values pack a 3-bit type tag with a 5-bit small length or integer into one byte. The largest benchmark gaps, such as ESLint at 64 B schema-driven vs 969 B schema-less, come from schema-typed object and array encodings, which the C++ compiler does not generate yet.
when_to_use: Payloads crossing metered, slow or lossy links (mobile, IoT, constrained radio), where bytes on the wire cost more than CPU cycles. This is the use case the README names.

Small to medium JSON messages, from tens of bytes to a few KB, where general-purpose compression does not pay off. On all 27 benchmark documents, the schema-driven output was smaller than JSON compressed with GZIP -9, LZ4 -12 or LZMA -9.

You already keep JSON Schema 2020-12 definitions (for example in OpenAPI or AsyncAPI) with tight constraints (bounded integers, enums, const, string length bounds) and want to reuse them instead of writing Protobuf or Avro schemas. That is the enum-heavy, Zod-generated-schema storage use case raised in issue #896.

Storing or sending many schema-conforming records where repeated string values dominate. Even schema-less, string deduplication gave TravisCI config 185 B vs MessagePack 627 B, and .NET project 748 B vs 919 B (benchmark page).

Integer, number and enum payloads you can encode with the C++ code today. For fully schema-driven objects, the benchmarked Apache-2.0 TypeScript prototype (npm jsonbinpack, archived) is the implementation that has those encoders.
when_not_to_use: Latency- or throughput-bound paths (IPC, intra-datacenter RPC, zero-copy reads). The README itself points these to FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto. The repo has no speed benchmark, and decoding always builds a sourcemeta::core::JSON DOM.

You need the benchmark's schema-driven sizes from C++ today. The compiler maps only integer, number and enum/const schemas; object, array and string schemas fall back to schema-less encoding. The status page lists those mappers and nine object/array/string encodings as missing, and the e2e tests cover schema-less only ('TODO: Test schema-driven too'). The maintainer wrote in issue #896 that this repo is not at feature parity with the JS prototype.
Schemas that rely on $ref, allOf/anyOf/oneOf, if/then/else, dependentSchemas, unevaluated* or recursion. The project's status page lists all of these as not covered yet.

Decoding untrusted bytes. The README calls decoding non-conforming data undefined behavior. Index and range checks in the decoder are assert()s, which disappear in release builds (for example BYTE_CHOICE_INDEX indexes the choices vector unchecked). The repo has no fuzz tests.

Schema-less-only use as a MessagePack replacement for tiny documents: the gain is often zero. From the benchmark page data, schema-less mode ties MessagePack byte-for-byte on 10 of 27 documents (e.g. TSLint 51 B vs 51 B) and ESLint is 969 B vs 971 B. Also skip it for closed-source network services that cannot accept AGPL-3.0 and will not buy the commercial license.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake, BUILD_SHARED_LIBS), in two components: runtime (encoder/decoder) and compiler (schema to encoding)
integration.dependencies: Sourcemeta Core (json, uri, jsonpointer, jsonschema, numeric, regex, io) and Sourcemeta Blaze (alterschema, canonicalizer), both vendored and pinned by commit in DEPENDENCIES. Core in turn vendors PCRE2 and mimalloc, which is linked into executables on Linux/macOS unless SOURCEMETA_CORE_USE_SYSTEM_ALLOCATOR is set.
integration.min_toolchain: C++23 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23 from vendored Core defaults). The top level declares CMake 3.16, but vendored Core requires 3.24. CI builds on current GitHub runners with GCC and Clang on Ubuntu, Clang on macOS and MSVC on Windows. No minimum compiler versions are documented.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows per CI (static and shared builds, plus ASan/UBSan jobs). No architecture-specific code was seen in src/.
integration.thread_safety: not documented. Encoder and Decoder are stateful wrappers over one std::ostream/std::istream, and the Encoder owns a string back-reference cache. Use one instance per thread and stream (inferred from headers).

gotchas: The Encoder's string cache survives across write() calls. A string repeated in a later document on the same Encoder is written as a backward offset into an earlier document's bytes. Create a fresh Encoder per message if each message must decode on its own (inferred from runtime_encoder.h and cache.cc).
Resolving shared strings makes the Decoder seek backwards (InputStream::rewind calls seek), so it needs a seekable std::istream. Buffer forward-only socket data first.

Validate against the schema before encoding. The encoder checks bounds, multipleOf and string lengths with assert() only, so in NDEBUG builds an out-of-range value in an 8-bit encoding is silently cast to uint8_t instead of rejected. compile() also mutates the schema you pass in.

Sizes from this C++ repo won't match the published benchmark. The e2e fixtures show schema-less sizes equal to the prototype's on some documents (ESLint 969 B, package.json 1,957 B), slightly larger on others (GeoJSON 127 vs 117 B; JSON Resume 2,619 vs 2,612 B, where a TODO notes Smile's 2,613 B now wins) and smaller on Road Risk (254 vs 261 B). Wire compatibility with npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x is not documented.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over fernBuffer or qdf when your data is already described by JSON Schema and you want the fewest bytes per small document from schema-level savings (enums, bounded integers, constants, string dedup), not a MessagePack-style or compression-tier layout. Pick Bebop, SBE, rkyv or YaFF instead when encode/decode latency is what you are buying, because JSON BinPack publishes no speed numbers at all.
verified_claims_summary: This is a size result only: on the author's json-size-benchmark (27 SchemaStore documents, one per JSON Taxonomy class), the archived TypeScript prototype (npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x) in schema-driven mode produced the smallest or tied-smallest uncompressed encoding against Protobuf 3.12.4, FlatBuffers 1.12.0, Cap'n Proto 0.7.0, MessagePack 1.0.0, Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile and FlexBuffers (e.g. ESLint config 64 B vs Avro 100 B, Protobuf 161 B, JSON 1,141 B), and it beat GZIP/LZ4/LZMA-compressed JSON on all 27 documents. Compiler and hardware are irrelevant for byte counts, no speed was measured, and the C++ code in this repo is not what was benchmarked.
status_note: Flagged active, but since late 2024 nearly all commits are Core/Blaze dependency bumps (last encoding work October 2024, README revised August 2026), with no tagged releases and a single contributor; the code is copyable under AGPL-3.0-or-later or a paid commercial license, and the benchmarked TypeScript prototype is archived but Apache-2.0.
